en: The Apadāna of the Elder Upāli Buddhavagga 8. Upālittheraapadāna
“In the city of Haṃsavatī,
there was a brahmin named Sujāta,
who possessed a hoard of eight hundred million [pieces of gold].”
Possessing abundant wealth and grain,
a reciter who has mastered the mantras,
one who has gone to the further shore of the three Vedas;
He has reached perfection in the science of marks, in history, and in his own doctrine.
He is a wanderer with a single topknot.
The Gotamas were disciples of the Buddha,
while the Carakas and the ascetics likewise wandered upon the earth at that time.
"A renowned brahmin surrounds me on all sides;
many people pay me honor."
I did not honor anyone;
I saw no one worthy of honor,
for at that time I was arrogant with pride.
The word "Buddha" does not exist as long as a Conqueror has not yet arisen;
it occurs only after the passing of a day and night.
Named Padumuttara;
having dispelled all darkness,
he arose in the world as one possessed of vision.
When the teaching had become widespread, well-known, and extensive,
the Buddha then approached.
In the city named Haṃsavatī,
that Buddha, the Visionary One, taught the Dhamma for the sake of his father.
At that time, the assembly extended for a league all around;
he was highly esteemed by men.
A ascetic named Sunanda then covered the entire assembly of the Buddha with flowers.
While he, the Supreme One, was proclaiming the Four Noble Truths in the Flower Pavilion,
[to] one hundred thousand times ten million [beings],...
There was a realization of the Dhamma.
Having rained down showers of Dhamma for seven nights and days, the Buddha—
When the eighth day had arrived,
the Jina praised Sunanda, saying:
"Whether in the world of the gods or among humans,"
Wandering through existence,
he will pass from one state of being to another, becoming the most eminent among all beings.
In a hundred thousand aeons,
one born of the Okkāka clan,
known by the family name Gotama, will appear.
A Teacher shall appear in the world.
His heir in the Dhammas,
his own legitimate son, fashioned by the Dhamma;
"Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī,
will become a disciple of the Teacher.
Thus did the Fully Awakened One praise him.
Then, making all the people laugh, he displayed his own power to the ascetic Sunanda.
People, with palms joined in reverence, pay homage to the ascetic Sunanda,
having performed an act of merit toward the Buddha.
He purified his own destination.
Having heard the words of the Sage, this was my resolve there:
"I too shall do service so that I may see Gotama.
Having thought thus, I—
I reflected upon my actions:
"What deed shall I perform in this unsurpassed field of merit?"
And this monk Pāṭhika,
among all reciters in the teaching,
was placed at the very head in the Vinaya.
I aspire to that state.
This immeasurable wealth of mine is unshakable, like the ocean.
With that wealth, I had a monastery built for the Buddha;
it was a beautiful monastery named Sobhana.
To the east of the city,
having purchased it for one hundred thousand,
I had a monastery built.
Having constructed gabled halls, palaces,
pavilions, watchtowers, and caves,
as well as well-constructed walkways,
I had a monastery built,
as well as a sauna, a fire hall,
and a water pavilion.
Having had a bathhouse built,
I gave it to the community of monks,
as well as couches and chairs.
For personal use and for vessels,
as well as for monastery attendants and medicine—
I gave all of this.
Having established a guard,
I had a strong wall built,
so that no one might harm him.
For those of peaceful mind and equanimity,
I had a residence built in the Saṅghārāma at a cost of one hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Having measured out that vast space,
I presented it to the Sambuddha;
thus was my monastery completed by me.
Please accept it, O Sage;
I shall lead you forth, O Hero—
consent to this, O Visionary One.
Padumuttara, the knower of the world,
the recipient of offerings,
having understood my intention,
The Leader consented.
Having understood the consent of the All-Knowing Great Sage, [the assembly rejoiced].
Having prepared the meal,
I announced that it was time.
When the time had been announced,
The Leader Padumuttara,
accompanied by a thousand monks whose taints were exhausted,
came to my monastery.
Knowing that he was seated,
I satisfied him with food and drink;
knowing that he had finished eating, I...
I spoke these words:
"He was purchased for a hundred thousand,
and for that same amount he was made to work."
"It is a beautiful park;
accept it, O Sage. By this gift of a park,"
And through my volitions and aspirations,
as I am being reborn in existence,
I obtain what I have desired.
Having accepted the well-constructed monastic park for the Saṅgha, the Perfectly Enlightened One sat down amidst the community of bhikkhus.
He spoke these words:
"He who gave to the Buddha that well-constructed monastery for the Saṅgha..."
I shall praise that;
listen as I speak.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—
And a fourfold army shall constantly surround him;
this is the fruit of this monastery for the Sangha.
Sixty thousand well-adorned lutes and drums shall constantly attend upon him.
This is the fruit of the monastery:
sixty-eight thousand women,
beautifully adorned.
Adorned with various garments and ornaments,
wearing jeweled earrings,
with long, reddish-brown eyes and a smiling face.
Well-proportioned with slender waists,
they shall always attend upon me;
this is the fruit of the Saṅghārāma.
For thirty thousand aeons he will delight in the world of the gods;
a thousand times he will be the Lord of Devas.
He will exercise sovereignty over the gods.
He will obtain everything that is to be obtained by a king of the gods.
Having possessed inexhaustible enjoyment,
he will exercise sovereignty over the gods;
a thousand times he will be a wheel-turning monarch.
He will become a king over the realm;
his sovereignty over the earth will be vast,
beyond all calculation.
In a hundred thousand aeons hence,
one born of the Okkāka clan,
known by the family name Gotama, will appear.
A Teacher shall appear in the world.
His heir in the Dhammas,
his own legitimate son, fashioned from the Dhamma;
One named Upāli by name will become a disciple of the Teacher;
having reached perfection in the Vinaya, he will be known as the foremost among those who uphold the discipline.
Skilled in what is possible and impossible,
upholding the teaching of the Victor,
he will dwell free from taints.
Having directly known all this,
Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans,
sat down amidst the community of bhikkhus.
He will place me at the very head [of his disciples].
From this time forth, throughout immeasurable aeons,
I shall aspire to your teaching.
Thus has my goal been attained:
the destruction of all fetters.
Just like a man impaled upon a stake,
Defeated by royal punishment,
finding no comfort even on the stake,
he desires only release.
In the same way, O Great Hero,
I have been struck by the staff of existence; being pierced by the stake of karma, I remain.
Afflicted by the sensation of thirst,
I find no pleasure in existence,
burning with the three fires.
I seek deliverance,
like one punished by a king’s decree,
like a man overcome by poison.
Afflicted by poison,
he would seek an antidote as a means to destroy that poison.
Searching, he might see an antidote that destroys poison;
having drunk it, he would become happy.
For the sake of complete liberation from poison.
In that same way, O Great Hero,
as a man who has been poisoned [seeks relief], so do I [seek you].
Oppressed by ignorance,
I sought the medicine of the True Dhamma;
seeking that medicine of the Dhamma, I—
I have seen the teaching of the Sakyan:
it is the foremost of all medicines,
the remover of every dart.
Having drunk the medicine of the Dhamma,
I have eradicated all poison;
[I have attained] the state of coolness, free from aging and death.
I touched Nibbāna—
just as a person who stands upon reality,
though oppressed by a grasp of the unreal.
One should seek a physician for the sake of liberation from what has become [suffering].
While seeking, one might see—
To him who is skilled in the sciences of spirits,
that spirit shall flee and he shall destroy it along with its root.
In the same way, O Great Hero,
oppressed by that grasping at "I," I seek the light of knowledge.
For the sake of complete liberation from that darkness,
I then saw the Sage of the Sakyas,
the purifier of the darkness of defilements.
Thus he dispelled my darkness,
like a physician treating a disease;
I cut through the stream of saṃsāra.
I have dammed the stream of craving;
I have uprooted all existence,
just as a physician of beings [extracts] it from the root.
Just as a garuḍa swoops down upon its prey,
a serpent, from all around within a hundred yojanas, so does he descend.
He agitates the great lake;
having seized the serpent,
he torments it with its head hanging downward.
Taking it, that bird departs,
flying wherever it desires;
even so am I, O Great Hero.
Just as a powerful garuḍa,
seeking the unconditioned,
has now washed away my faults.
I have seen the excellent Dhamma,
the unsurpassed state of peace;
taking it up, may I dwell in this.
Just as a garuḍa [seizes] a serpent,
there is a creeper named Āsāvatī,
born in the Cittalatāvana grove.
For her, one fruit ripens in a thousand years;
the gods attend upon it.
While its fruit is so far off,
this *āsāvatī* creeper is nevertheless beloved by the gods as the best of creepers.
Having taken up [this task] for a hundred thousand years,
I shall attend upon that Sage;
evening and morning I pay homage.
Just as the gods [protect] this world,
so too service is not in vain,
and veneration is never fruitless.
Though I have come from afar,
this moment has not failed me;
I see no further rebirth.
Searching through existence,
I am now free from acquisitions, liberated,
and dwelling in peace.
Just as the lotus named Paduma blossoms by the rays of the sun,
even so do I, O Great Hero.
It has blossomed through the Buddha’s radiance.
Just as in the womb of a crane,
a male chick is never found;
When the clouds thunder,
they always conceive;
they carry the fetus for a long time.
As long as the cloud does not thunder,
people are burdened; they are liberated from their burdens when the cloud pours down rain.
Of the Buddha Padumuttara,
as he roared with the rain-cloud of Dhamma;
by the sound of that Dhamma-rain-cloud,
I did not conceive a womb of Dhamma.
Having taken up a hundred thousand [lives],
I have borne a womb of merit.
I am not released from the burden;
the cloud of Dhamma does not thunder.
But when you, O Sakyan Sage, [do so]...
Delighting in Kapilavatthu,
you thunder with the cloud of Dhamma,
O Bhāratī, as I am being completely liberated.
Emptiness and the signless,
as well as the wishless;
and all four fruits—
Thus I understood the Dhamma.
Second Recitation Section.
From an immeasurable time past...
I aspire to your teaching;
that goal of mine has been attained—
the unsurpassed state of peace.
I have reached perfection in the Vinaya,
just like the seer Pāṭhika;
there is no one equal to me.
I uphold the teaching:
both the Vinaya and the Khandhakas,
and the Tikaccheda as the fifth.
In this matter I have no doubt,
whether regarding the vowels or the consonants;
nor do I have any doubt concerning the refutation or the counter-argument.
Skilled in what is possible and impossible,
he has reached perfection in all matters regarding reinstatement and formal emergence from probation.
Having set down the words in either the Vinaya or the Khandhaka,
and having unraveled them from both sides, I [shall explain].
I would descend [into the depths] by way of flavor;
being well-skilled in etymology and proficient in what is meaningful and what is meaningless.
"There is nothing unknown to me;
I am one-pointed in the Teacher's dispensation.
Today I am a seer of forms."
In the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans,
I dispel all doubt and cut through every uncertainty.
The line, and also the following line,
the syllable, and also the phoneme;
at the beginning and at the conclusion.
I am skilled in all respects,
just as a powerful king,
having subdued his enemies, oppresses those who strike back.
Having conquered the battle,
he should have a city built there,
complete with a rampart and a moat.
He should have watchtowers and gatehouses built,
as well as many various kinds of palatial towers throughout the city.
One should have a crossroads and a square built,
with well-arranged market stalls,
and a public hall there.
The discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful,
for the purpose of destroying enemies,
and to know their vulnerabilities and strengths.
For the protection of his own body,
he appoints a general;
for the protection of his goods, he appoints a guard.
He appoints a guardian of his goods, saying, "May my property not be lost," to a man skilled in its safekeeping.
He gives legal authority to one who is devoted to the king and whom he desires to see prosper.
One should act as a friend toward one who is skilled in portents, omens, and bodily marks.
He appoints a reciter who retains the mantras to the position of family priest.
Endowed with these qualities, he—
He is called a Khattiya;
they always protect the king,
even when he is suffering, like a ruddy goose.
In the same way, O Great Hero,
you are like a kṣatriya who has slain his enemies,
[the victor] over the world including the devas.
He is called the King of Dhamma.
Having utterly defeated the heretics and Māra together with his host, he is so named.
Having dispelled that darkness,
he built the city of Dhamma; there,
virtue served as the rampart wall.
Knowledge is your gateway-tower;
faith is your pillar, O Hero,
and restraint is your doorkeeper.
The watchtower is the foundations of mindfulness,
O Sage; wisdom is your crossroads,
and the bases of psychic power are your meeting place.
The path of the Dhamma has been well-laid out:
the Suttanta, the Abhidhamma,
and the Vinaya in its entirety.
The ninefold word of the Buddha—
this is your true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva):
emptiness and signlessness.
The sublime dwelling, the imperturbable, and cessation—
this is your Dhamma-cottage.
Foremost in wisdom,
skilled in ready wit,
known by the name of Sāriputta.
You are the General of the Dhamma,
skilled in death and rebirth,
and have reached the perfection of supernormal power.
O Sage, he who was formerly your family priest was named Kolita;
he was a bearer of the ancient lineage.
Of exalted power and difficult to approach,
foremost in the quality of being a proponent of the ascetic practices (dhuta),
you are the one who beholds with the eye of wisdom— homage to you, O Sage!
One who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma,
and one who has mastered all the teachings in the Dispensation—
Ānanda by name.
"O Sage, you are my protector of the Dhamma.
Having transcended all these,
the Blessed One has sent me forth."
He gave me a decision according to the Vinaya as proclaimed by the wise;
whoever has a question regarding the Vinaya—
The disciple of the Buddha asks this;
I have no thought regarding it—
how can I explain that very matter?
To whatever extent there is within the Buddha-field,
excluding that Great Sage,
there is no one like me in the Vinaya.
What more could there be?
Seated in the community of monks,
Gotama thunders thus.
There is no one equal to Upāli in the Vinaya and the Khandhakas,
as far as that which was spoken by the Buddha extends.
The Teacher’s dispensation has nine branches;
all that is the depth of the Vinaya for one who perceives the root of the Vinaya.
Having remembered my deed,
Gotama, the bull of the Sakyans,
sat down amidst the community of bhikkhus.
He placed me at the very head [of his disciples].
For a hundred thousand years,
I aspired for this state.
Thus my purpose has been attained;
I have reached perfection in the Vinaya.
I am the bringer of joy to the Sakyans.
Formerly, I was a barber;
having abandoned that birth,
I am now born as the son of the Great Sage.
In this second aeon,
there was a kṣatriya named Añjasa,
possessed of infinite splendor and immeasurable fame.
Bhūmipāla was a man of great wealth.
I am the son of that king,
a kshatriya named Candana.
Proud of his birth, and intoxicated by the pride of fame and wealth—
[he encountered] hundreds of thousands of nāgas.
Adorned with every ornament,
elephants that exude ichor from three places always surround me.
Surrounded by my companions,
desiring to go to the pleasure grove,
I mounted the elephant Sirika.
I then departed from the city,
endowed with moral conduct,
guarding the doors of my senses, and well-restrained.
The Sambuddha named Devala came before me;
having dispatched the nāga named Sirika, he arrived.
I then provoked the Buddha;
thereupon, that enraged nāga did not lift his foot.
Seeing the naga with a wicked mind,
I gave way to anger toward the Buddha;
having harassed the Fully Enlightened One, I...
I went to the garden,
yet I found no pleasure there,
for it was as if my head were ablaze.
I am burning with feverish passion,
like a fish caught on a hook;
the earth, bounded by the ocean, [is my domain].
I felt as if I were on fire;
approaching my father’s presence,
I spoke these words.
Like an enraged venomous snake,
like a mass of fire that has arrived,
like a rutting elephant with its tusks—
I have encountered the Self-Existent One.
I have encountered the Buddha, the Fierce One,
the Victor of Exalted Austerity.
"Otherwise we shall all perish;
we will ask that sage for forgiveness.
If we do not appease him,"
"One who has tamed himself and is composed—
within seven days,
he will bring my kingdom to ruin."
Sumekhalo, Kosiya,
Siggava, and Sattaka—
having assailed these seers,
Wretched are those people of their own country when the seers—
self-restrained and living the holy life— become angry.
They destroy the world together with its gods,
its oceans, and its mountains,
throughout three thousand yojanas.
I assembled the men and,
for the purpose of confessing my transgression,
I approached the Self-Existent One.
With all their limbs and all their veins visible,
everyone with palms joined in reverence,
having prostrated at the feet of the Buddha,
They spoke these words:
"Forgive us, O Great Hero;
the people are entreating you."
Dispel this fever;
do not destroy our kingdom.
All beings, including gods and humans—
May the Dānavas together with the Rakkhasas always split my head with an iron mallet.
Fire does not remain in water,
a seed does not grow on a rock,
and a worm does not remain in an antidote.
Anger does not arise toward the Buddha.
Just as the earth is immovable and the ocean is immeasurable;
And space is infinite;
likewise, the Buddhas are unshakable.
Always patient, they are great heroes.
And the ascetics have been forgiven;
for those who are patient and have forgiven,
that departure does not exist.
Having said this, the Fully Awakened One,
dispelling the fever of the great multitude before them, [spoke].
Then it rose up into the sky.
Because of that deed, O Hero,
I have fallen into a state of inferiority.
Having transcended that birth,
I entered the city free from fear.
Even then, O Great Hero, you...
While it was burning, well-composed,
I dispelled the fever and asked the Self-Become One for forgiveness.
Even now, O Great Hero,
you have extinguished the three fires that were burning me.
And he attained the state of coolness.
Listen to me as I speak, you who have the ear to attend.
I shall declare the goal to you,
just as I have seen that state for myself.
Having disparaged that Self-Existent One,
With a peaceful mind and concentrated,
yet because of that very karma,
I am today born into a lowly womb.
Do not let this opportune moment pass you by,
for those who have missed the moment grieve;
strive instead for your own true welfare.
The opportunity has been provided for you:
for some there is emesis,
and for others purgation.
To some it is the virulent halāhala poison,
while to others it is medicine; for those who have undertaken the practice of emesis, it is the means of purification.
The fruit is the purgative for those established in the fruits;
it is the medicine for those seeking the attainment of fruits,
and the field of merit for those who seek it.
To those who oppose the Teaching,
it is like the halāhala poison,
like a venomous snake whose gaze is poisonous.
In this way it consumes that man.
Once drunk, the halāhala poison cuts short one's life.
Having violated the Teaching,
one burns for ten million eons;
[but by] patience and non-violence...
And by possessing a mind of loving-kindness,
he delivers the world together with its devas;
therefore, you should be non-contentious.
They do not cling to gain or loss,
nor to honor or dishonor;
the Buddhas are like the earth.
Therefore, you have no enmity toward Devadatta, the murderer,
the thief Aṅgulimāla, or anyone else.
Toward both Rāhula and Dhanapāla,
the Sage was equal toward all;
in them, he had no aversion.
No passion exists within me;
the Buddha is equal toward all,
whether toward a murderer or toward his own son.
Having seen the saffron robe discarded on the ground, smeared with filth,
he placed his palms together in reverence upon his head.
The lineage of the accomplished ones is to be honored.
Those Buddhas who have passed away,
those who are present, and those yet to come—
By this banner they are purified;
therefore, these are worthy of homage.
The Teacher’s system is well-disciplined.
I bear [the Vinaya] in my heart;
paying homage to the Vinaya,
I shall dwell at all times.
The Vinaya is my dwelling place;
the Vinaya is my standing and walking ground;
I make my abode in the Vinaya.
The Vinaya is my domain.
I have reached perfection in the Vinaya and am skilled in meditative tranquility as well.
Upāli, O Great Hero,
pays homage at the feet of the Teacher.
Thus shall I wander.
From village to village, from city to city,
he went paying homage to the Fully Awakened One and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma.
The defilements have been incinerated by me;
all states of existence have been uprooted;
all taints are completely exhausted.
Now there is no further becoming.
Welcome indeed has come to me in the presence of the Best of Buddhas.
The three true insights have been attained;
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical knowledges—
And these eight liberations have been realized; the six direct knowledges have been attained;
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
Thus indeed the venerable elder Upāli spoke these verses.
This is the sixth legend of the elder Upāli.
